jestina.tldr: Most revenue came from search, while the display ads (DA) meant to create new demand was scattered across agencies. I brought DA operations into one place and allocated budget by customer stage rather than channel efficiency. On the same closing report, GA4 ROAS rose from 352% in May 2025 to 583% in July.
jestina.cardProblem: Revenue was concentrated in search, where customers who already knew the brand came in, and the display ads (DA) meant to bring in new customers ran separately at each agency.
jestina.cardDecision: I brought DA into one place, gave each customer stage its own channels, and split the budget by those roles.

jestina.detail.overview: I started reading the revenue search protects separately from the new demand DA has to create. I brought scattered DA operations into one place and reallocated the annual budget by customer stage.
jestina.detail.challenge: Revenue was there, but growth had stalled. DA was already running, but each channel sat with a different agency, and the work stopped at making and uploading creatives. With no one looking across channels, no combined insight came out, and most revenue sat in search, where customers who already knew the brand came in.
jestina.detail.dataAnalysis: Once the scattered channels ran in one place, I could see what had been invisible: how keywords and creatives related, and even viral and external factors moving outside the ad platforms, all on one screen. I cross-checked GA4 against media data to separate repeat customers from new visitors. Search was strong at capturing repeat purchases but contributed little to new demand. Ranking channels on efficiency alone gave no reason to move budget.
jestina.detail.strategy: First I put operations under one owner so learning could build across channels. Then I split the budget by customer stage: DA took Awareness, Shopping and Search took Consideration, and Brand Search and Search took Conversion, each with its own KPI.

newbalance.headline: I linked inventory to ads automatically, so budget stopped leaking into sold-out products.
newbalance.tldr: Checking 10 channels and hundreds of SKUs from memory had limits. I automated inventory, spend-pacing and creative checks, cutting internal check time from ~2 hours to under 5 minutes, and set stop conditions so ads aren't touched when the data looks wrong.
newbalance.cardProblem: People checked the stock of hundreds of products across 10 channels one by one, so responses to stock-outs were slow and errors were frequent.
newbalance.cardDecision: I connected inventory lookups to pausing sold-out creatives. If a lookup fails or the scope doesn't match, the run ends without changing any ads.

newbalance.detail.overview: Running 10 channels and hundreds of SKUs that change every season, I built automation that cuts repeated checks and stops running when the data is wrong.
newbalance.detail.challenge: Even with ROAS that looked good, showing sold-out products or letting spend stall cost money. When I took over, the owner opened the site page by page to check stock, and doing it by hand led to frequent errors. Internal checks took about 2 hours a day; the public MOP case study of the same task put the manual average at about 3 hours. I started automating so the time saved could go into finding insights.
newbalance.detail.dataAnalysis: Before cutting check time, I counted what we were missing. When people check hundreds of SKUs across 10 channels from memory, stock-outs and stalled spend were always noticed a beat late, and ad spend kept going out in the meantime. So I set the automation's goal on how quickly a problem gets noticed.
newbalance.detail.strategy: I didn't judge budget on media ROAS alone; I split the operating rules to look at stock status, search demand and each channel's role together. I blocked duplicate runs, stale data and matching errors first, and made the system stop before touching ads when abnormal data came in.

Once the samples were matched, CVR and CPA had actually improved, and the real bottleneck was closer to the consultation form than to the creatives. In round two I brought back one qualifying question, and in round three I changed the question order to move the drop-off point. The form that maximizes CVR and the form that protects lead quality were different forms. gangwon.detail.overview: Before explaining results, I aligned the period, media, billing and conversion standards. After recalculating on one scope, I broke results down by product, media and month, and made ad-driven revenue and group-buy revenue readable separately.
gangwon.detail.challenge: Existing reports differed on whether Payco was included and how conversion change was written, so comparing big numbers as they were risked explaining the results wrongly. On top of that, as group buys grew, the gap between total store revenue and ad-driven revenue widened, and mixing the two could over- or understate ad performance.
gangwon.detail.dataAnalysis: I compared January 1 – June 30, 2026 with the same period last year on the same media scope. I fixed the basis to excluding VAT, completed purchases and excluding Payco, recalculated spend and conversion revenue on that scope, and confirmed ROAS of 237.95%. Then I broke it down by month, product and media to narrow where growth came from. H1 growth was driven by Shopping Search (revenue +107.4%), supported by GFA-ADVoost retargeting. Brand search, by contrast, lost 32% of conversions while impressions and clicks held, so lost demand didn't explain it. July 2026 store sales came from a 402.3% rise in orders with the average order value almost flat (−1.0%), and 5 of the top 7 products were group-buy products (44.7% of sales).
gangwon.detail.strategy: First I made every report use the same numerator and denominator, then narrowed causes down to product and media. I didn't credit the rise to a single action either; I recorded separately that turning off MOP, switching to manual bids and product-level changes all happened together. Whether to use automated bidding depends on the account's conditions, not on which tool is better. With many products and enough conversions to learn from, automated bidding wins; but with few products and conversions bunched into group-buy windows like this account, the learning signal can be skewed, so I judged fixed manual bids to be more stable. For the brand search drop, I set a hypothesis that purchases may have spread across group buys, influencer links and direct store visits, and chose to split measurement rather than cut channels. On the sales side, I judged that search and shopping ads could only capture so much demand, so I opened a new purchase path with Instagram group-buys. During group-buy periods I ran influencer partnership ads alongside.

dyson.detail.overview: I connected the subscriber campaign, product-experience content and live commerce into one operating flow. I judged by whether content led to the next action rather than by raw views, and adjusted the media mix by comparing DP and video CTR and CPC on the same basis.
dyson.detail.challenge: Premium appliances are high-involvement products with long research before purchase. But subscriber growth, content viewing and live-commerce traffic were each run separately, so each campaign's role and the next action were unclear. In early February, I also found more budget going to display (DP) ads, which were performing worse.
dyson.detail.dataAnalysis: The December 2023 subscription campaign recorded 104,257 conversions at a CPA of about KRW 1,132. Comparing formats in February 2024 showed a clear gap: DP at CTR 0.73% and CPC KRW 637, video at CTR 2.16% and CPC KRW 160. I used this comparison as the basis for reallocating budget.
dyson.detail.strategy: First I redefined what counts as performance. Views alone couldn't tell whether the thumbnail or the content was weak, so I split impressions, product clicks and 10-second-plus views into separate metrics. Then I separated the purpose and KPI of subscription conversion, content learning and live traffic. I compared formats over the same period and metrics, and concentrated budget on video once its efficiency was confirmed. Community posts carried the broadcast benefit and product name so viewers moved on to join the live.

dyson.detail.learnings: I should separate campaign purposes first, compare formats on one basis, and only then move budget. Separating learning and stable periods, and running content, community and live as one flow, let me manage channel assets and short-term results together.

automation.headline: I moved the inventory checks, reports and settlement people used to repeat into six automations.
automation.tldr: I automated work that had to be checked over and over — inventory, spend pacing, landing pages, reports and settlement. The setup cuts the time spent gathering data so the time goes to operating decisions and planning. All six tools run only after their input data passes validation.

automation.cardProblem: As repeat checks piled up, gathering data took longer than finding what was actually wrong.
automation.cardDecision: I automated the work, but first set the stop conditions so it runs only when the data is sound.

automation.detail.overview: I planned, built and operated six systems that check inventory, spend pacing, landing pages, reports and settlement on a fixed schedule. They were applied across several brands including New Balance, and I wrote the run scripts and operating documents so whoever takes over can pick them up right away.
automation.detail.challenge: Too much work depended on someone remembering to check. Checking late meant wasted ad spend; spending time on checks left no time for decisions.
automation.detail.dataAnalysis: I started by counting what could go wrong. Even if inventory collection only half succeeds, the decision logic still runs. Then products that are still in stock read as sold out and their ads get switched off. The danger wasn't the system stopping — it was the system carrying on.
automation.detail.strategy: I put safeguards ahead of speed. If any one of these is detected — a missing reference file, zero samples, too high a share of unknown stock, or too high a collection failure rate — the job stops without touching ads and alerts the person in charge.
